canonicalExplanation.summary: When several declarations target the same property of the same element, the **cascade** picks a winner by checking, in order: (1) **origin and importance** — browser defaults, user styles, author styles, and `!important` flipping that order; (2) **cascade layers** (`@layer`) — later layers beat earlier ones; (3) **specificity**; (4) **source order**. Specificity only matters when the earlier steps tie.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A design system puts reset styles, base styles and component styles in layers. A developer writes a super-specific selector in the base layer — and a plain class in the components layer still beats it. Surprising, until you know the order of the cascade. A low-specificity rule in a later author layer can beat a highly specific rule in an earlier layer. In this lesson you'll determine the winning declaration in a layered multi-origin example.

```predict
{"question": "`@layer base, components;` — `#nav a.link` (base) vs `.link` (components). Which colour wins?", "options": ["The #nav rule — it's more specific", "The .link rule — its layer comes later"], "answer": 1, "why": "Layer order is checked before specificity. A later layer wins even with a weaker selector (for normal, non-important declarations)."}
```

examples.title: A later layer beats a specific selector
examples.situation: A low-specificity rule in a later author layer can beat a highly specific rule in an earlier layer.
walkthrough: **Layers:** `@layer reset, base, components;` declares the order.
**Compare:** `#nav a.link` sits in base (earlier); `.link` sits in components (later). Both are normal author declarations.
**Check order:** origin ties, so layers decide before specificity — the browser will render `.link` as navy.
examples.result: The link is navy: the later layer wins before specificity is even considered.

examples.title: The user's large-text setting
examples.situation: A user stylesheet sets `body { font-size: 24px !important; }`; the site sets `body { font-size: 14px !important; }`.
walkthrough: Both are !important, so importance flips origin order.
Important user styles beat important author styles.
The user's 24px wins — protecting users who need larger text.
examples.result: The page renders at 24px because important user declarations outrank important author ones.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Specificity is always the first and strongest cascade factor.
misconceptions.correction: The cascade checks origin and importance first, then cascade layers, and only then specificity, with source order last. A weak selector in a later layer can beat a very specific one in an earlier layer.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "A later layer beats a specific selector", which step decided the winner?

analogy.example: The cascade is like a **tournament with rounds**: first by league (origin/importance), then by division (layer), then by score (specificity), then by who played last (order). A top scorer in a lower division never faces the division winner.
usefulFor: seeing specificity as a later round
limitations: Tournaments have one winner overall; the cascade runs per property per element.
!important is like a rule that reverses league rankings.

steps.explanation: Origin and importance tie, so the next step decides.
The later author layer wins before specificity is compared.
A low-specificity rule in a later author layer beats a highly specific rule in an earlier layer.

trace.textAlternative: Resolving a layered conflict. Step 1, Origin: both is author, normal. Origin and importance tie, so the next step decides. Step 2, Layers: base is earlier; components is later → wins. The later author layer wins before specificity is compared. Step 3, Result: color is navy. A low-specificity rule in a later author layer beats a highly specific rule in an earlier layer.
